title: Overview and justification
body:
By now you should be comfortable with the basics of referencing: naming sources, matching a style, and spotting an inconsistent citation. This course builds on that. It moves from getting referencing right to judging it: checking a paraphrase properly against its original, weighing whether a reference list's range reflects the real scope of someone's research, and working out how to reference a source that does not fit a standard template.

By the end you will be able to check a paraphrase against its source, judge whether a reference list's range reflects real research scope, and paraphrase a technical passage for a non-specialist reader. You will also work out what an unfamiliar source needs, reference it correctly under time pressure, and gather and cite sources that both support and challenge a position.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Analyse a paraphrase against its original source to check that no distinctive wording survives unattributed.
  • Evaluate a reference list to judge whether its range, including opposing views, reflects the genuine scope of the research undertaken.
  • Paraphrase a technical passage accurately for a non-specialist reader, marking any direct quotation and crediting the source throughout.
  • Analyse an unfamiliar source type to identify which elements a reader needs to locate it, rather than forcing it into a standard template.
  • Reference an unfamiliar source type correctly under time pressure, checking guidance and recording the decision so the approach can be repeated.
  • Gather and cite sources that both support and challenge a position, so a reader can judge the breadth of research behind a recommendation.

title: In real academic practice
body: Checking a paraphrase, judging a reference list's range, and working out how to cite something unfamiliar are not one-off exam skills: you will meet them across every module that asks for independent reading, from literature reviews to group projects with mixed source types. The judgement you build here also feeds directly into how you handle sources when researching and when writing critically, where the same questions about range, attribution and traceability come up again.

title: Signpost
body: The course has six short lessons. First, checking a paraphrase against its original source. Second, judging whether a reference list's range reflects real research scope. Third, paraphrasing a technical passage for a non-specialist reader. Fourth, working out what an unfamiliar source type needs. Fifth, referencing an unfamiliar source correctly under time pressure. Sixth, gathering and citing sources that support and challenge a position. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
instruction: Work through the six lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: This course moves from the mechanics of a reference to the judgement calls referencing demands. This lesson starts with paraphrase: writing an idea in your own words well enough that nothing of the original survives unattributed.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to compare a paraphrase against its source closely enough to catch wording that has survived, and to revise it so nothing has.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • compare a paraphrase against its original source
  • identify distinctive wording surviving unattributed in a paraphrase
  • revise a paraphrase so no wording survives unattributed

title: Concept: definition
body: A paraphrase restates an idea in the writer's own words and sentence structure, citing the source. Checking a paraphrase means comparing it sentence by sentence against the original, looking for any distinctive phrase, order or structure that has survived unattributed, even when the source is cited correctly. A citation credits the idea; it does not excuse wording that is still, in effect, the original author's.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen what a paraphrase needs to leave behind and what counts as wording surviving unattributed. The activities ahead let you practise spotting it and fixing it; the check at the end asks you to apply both.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Find a paraphrase you have written recently and put it side by side with its original source. Does any distinctive phrase or sentence structure survive?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to see how closely your own paraphrasing tracks the original.

title: Summary
body: You can now compare a paraphrase against its source, identify wording that has survived unattributed, and revise a paraphrase so nothing has. The next lesson turns to judging the range of a reference list as a whole.

_items.title: See pages 193 to 195 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: You have already checked that a reference list uses a consistent style and that each citation points to the right entry. This lesson asks a different question: does the list, taken as a whole, actually reflect the research it claims to draw on? A reference list can be perfectly formatted and still be thin, one-sided, or out of date, and none of that shows up in a style check.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not just reading a reference list; you are judging it. Given a reference list and the claim it is supposed to support, you will decide whether the list's range is wide enough, whether it includes views that disagree with the writer's own, and where the evidence coverage falls short.

title: Learning outcomes
body: A reference list earns a reader's trust by its range, not just its formatting. When you judge whether a reference list includes opposing views, whether its range matches its claimed scope, and where it leaves evidence gaps, you are reading the way an examiner or reviewer reads. You are checking for what the writer chose not to cite, as much as for what they did.

title: Moving into practice
body: Judging a reference list this way becomes second nature once you have done it a few times. Before you accept a reference list at face value, in your own reading or someone else's, ask what range it covers, whether disagreement is represented, and what it leaves out.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a reading list or reference list you have used recently, for an assignment or a piece of research. Does it include views that disagree with the argument it supports? Is there a gap in evidence coverage you noticed at the time, or only now? No right answers are expected here; the aim is to look at the list itself, not just the argument it was attached to.

title: Summary
body: A reference list's range matters as much as its formatting. Check whether it includes opposing views, whether its range matches the scope it claims, and where it leaves evidence gaps. A well-formatted list that fails all three still misrepresents the research behind it.

_items.title: See pages 191 to 193 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Referencing is no longer just about getting the mechanics right. You can now check a paraphrase against its source, judge whether a reference list's range reflects the real scope of someone's research, and paraphrase a technical passage for a non-specialist reader. You can also work out what an unfamiliar source needs, reference it correctly under time pressure, and gather sources that support and challenge a position. That judgement builds directly on the accuracy and consistency you brought from the introductory course. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: Apply this judgement the next time you draft a literature review or a group report with mixed source types. Check your own paraphrases against their originals, weigh whether your reading list's range reflects the scope of the question, and work out an unfamiliar source's citation from first principles rather than forcing it into a template. The same judgement about range and traceability is exactly what you draw on when finding and using sources for a longer project, and when researching a topic that calls for a documented method.

title: Where this goes next
body: This course has assumed the introductory groundwork: naming sources accurately, matching a style, and spotting an inconsistent citation. If any of that still feels shaky, the introductory course is there to revisit. Moving on, the advanced course in this pathway turns from getting the judgement right to acting on it under pressure: the ethical choices that referencing and attribution raise once you are working independently, in shared work, or in a professional role.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

body: A student rewrites a source sentence by swapping a few words but keeping its structure and most phrasing. What should checking the paraphrase against its original reveal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does checking a paraphrase against its original reveal here?

_items.text: That distinctive wording from the original survives unattributed, so it isn't yet a genuine paraphrase.
_items.feedback: Yes. Checking against the original shows whether its distinctive wording still survives unattributed.

_items.text: That the sentence is now too short to need a citation at all.
_items.feedback: Length doesn't remove the need to credit the source; wording and attribution do.

_items.text: That changing any words at all makes it sufficiently different from the source.
_items.feedback: A few swapped words can still leave the original's structure and phrasing intact.

_items.text: That the citation can simply move to the end of the paragraph instead.
_items.feedback: Where the citation sits doesn't address whether the wording is genuinely paraphrased.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Checking against the original shows whether its distinctive wording still survives unattributed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Compare the structure and phrasing, not just whether any words changed.

body: A reference list cites several sources that all support the same conclusion, with no opposing view represented. What does evaluating its range suggest?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does evaluating this reference list's range suggest?

_items.text: The range may not reflect the genuine scope of research into the topic.
_items.feedback: Yes. A one-sided list may understate how much research actually exists on the topic.

_items.text: The list is too short to meet a minimum reference count.
_items.feedback: Count alone doesn't show whether the research's real scope is reflected.

_items.text: The sources are too old to be considered current research.
_items.feedback: Age isn't stated here; the issue described is one-sidedness, not currency.

_items.text: The citation style used is inconsistent across the entries.
_items.feedback: Style consistency is a separate issue from whether the range reflects the topic's scope.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A list with no opposing view may not reflect the genuine scope of research into the topic.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what's missing from the list, not its length or style.

body: You are paraphrasing a technical passage for a reader unfamiliar with the field. What must the paraphrase still do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What must a technical paraphrase for a new reader still do?

_items.text: Credit the source throughout and mark any direct quotation, even in plain language.
_items.feedback: Yes. Simplifying the language doesn't remove the need to credit the source and mark any quotation.

_items.text: Avoid citing the source since the wording is now entirely your own.
_items.feedback: The ideas still come from the source, so it still needs crediting.

_items.text: Keep the original technical terms exactly as written, regardless of the reader.
_items.feedback: The task is to make the passage accessible, not to preserve every technical term.

_items.text: Cite the source once at the very end of the whole passage.
_items.feedback: A single end citation doesn't mark which parts are direct quotation throughout.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Even in plain language, the paraphrase must credit the source and mark any direct quotation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Simplifying the wording doesn't change what attribution the passage still needs.

body: You need to reference an unfamiliar source type with no obvious template. What should you identify first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you identify first for an unfamiliar source type?

_items.text: Which elements a reader would need to locate the source themselves.
_items.feedback: Yes. Starting from what a reader needs to locate the source works for any source type.

_items.text: Which existing template looks closest, even if it doesn't quite fit.
_items.feedback: Forcing an ill-fitting template risks leaving out what this source actually needs.

_items.text: Whether the source type is common enough to be worth citing.
_items.feedback: Commonness doesn't determine how to construct the reference itself.

_items.text: How many other students have cited the same source type before.
_items.feedback: Precedent from other students doesn't tell you what this reference needs.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Identifying what a reader needs to locate the source works from first principles, for any source type.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the reference is actually for, not which template is nearest.

body: You must reference an unfamiliar source type under time pressure. What should you do, beyond getting an answer quickly?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you do when referencing under time pressure?

_items.text: Check the guidance and record the decision so the approach can be repeated.
_items.feedback: Yes. Recording the decision means you don't have to work it out again next time.

_items.text: Use whichever format looks reasonable and move on without recording it.
_items.feedback: An unrecorded guess leaves you with nothing to check or repeat later.

_items.text: Skip the citation for now and add it only if someone asks.
_items.feedback: Skipping it risks the citation never being added at all.

_items.text: Copy the format used for a different, more familiar source type.
_items.feedback: Borrowing a format from an unrelated source type risks missing what this one needs.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Checking guidance and recording the decision means the approach can be repeated next time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you'd need the next time you meet the same source type.

body: A recommendation is backed only by sources that agree with it. What does gathering and citing opposing sources as well let a reader do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does citing opposing sources as well let a reader do?

_items.text: Judge the breadth of research behind the recommendation.
_items.feedback: Yes. Seeing both sides lets a reader judge how broad the research behind it really is.

_items.text: See that the recommendation has no real weaknesses at all.
_items.feedback: Citing opposing views doesn't remove weaknesses; it lets a reader weigh them.

_items.text: Assume the writer simply ran out of supporting evidence to cite.
_items.feedback: Including opposing sources is a deliberate choice, not a sign of running short.

_items.text: Skip reading the opposing sources, since they are only there for balance.
_items.feedback: They are there to be read and weighed, not skipped as decoration.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Citing sources on both sides lets a reader judge the real breadth of research behind the recommendation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reader gains from seeing opposing evidence included.

title: Activity: faithful paraphrase or surviving wording
body: Three paraphrases, each checked against its original sentence.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Classify each paraphrase as faithful or as having distinctive wording survive unattributed.

_items.text: Original: 'Students who log sources immediately cite more accurately.' Paraphrase: 'Dennis and Abbott (2026) found that recording sources straight away leads to more accurate citing.'

Original: 'A reference should give a reader everything needed to find the exact source.' Paraphrase: 'A reference should give a reader everything needed to find the exact source, according to Dennis and Abbott (2026).'

Original: 'Mixed citation styles force a reader to re-learn the pattern with every entry.' Paraphrase: 'When styles are mixed, Dennis and Abbott (2026) note that a reader must work out a fresh pattern for every entry.'

_feedback.correct: That's right. A citation does not excuse a sentence structure or phrase lifted almost word for word from the original.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Compare the sentence structure, not just the individual words, against the original.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of these are right, but not all. Check the rest.

title: Activity: steps for checking a paraphrase
body: These are the steps for checking a paraphrase against its source. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the steps for checking a paraphrase against its source in the correct order.

_items.text: Place the paraphrase next to the original passage.
Read both, sentence by sentence.
Mark any phrase or structure that closely tracks the original.
Rewrite each marked section in genuinely different wording and structure.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order: compare side by side first, read closely, mark what survives, then rewrite it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. You need both passages side by side before you can compare them. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some steps are in the right place, but not all. Try again.

title: Worked example: checking a paraphrase properly
displayTitle: Worked example: checking a paraphrase properly
body:
Two students each paraphrase the same sentence from a source and cite it.

{{learner-a}} swaps a few words for synonyms but keeps the original sentence structure almost exactly, then adds a citation at the end. The citation is correct, but the sentence is still, in effect, the original author's.

{{learner-b}} reads the original, closes the book, and writes the idea out in a different structure entirely, checking the result against the original afterward to confirm nothing distinctive has survived.

Only {{learner-b}}'s version is a genuine paraphrase; {{learner-a}}'s citation does not make a reworded original into one.

title: Activity: signs wording has survived
body: Four signs that distinctive wording has survived unattributed in a paraphrase. Select a card to flip it and see it explained.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

back.body: The order of clauses and ideas matches the original almost exactly, even if some words have changed.
A memorable or unusual turn of phrase from the original appears without quotation marks.
Individual words are replaced but the sentence otherwise reads the same as the original.
The same examples appear in the same order, suggesting the structure was copied rather than rethought.

title: Activity: revising a paraphrase properly
body: Four ways to revise a paraphrase so nothing survives unattributed. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Read, then write from memory
_items.body: Read the original, set it aside, and write the idea from memory rather than reworking the sentence in front of you.

_items.title: Change the structure, not just the words
_items.body: Reorder the clauses or combine separate sentences, rather than swapping words within the same structure.

_items.title: Quote anything you cannot improve on
_items.body: If a phrase genuinely cannot be bettered, put it in quotation marks instead of disguising it as a paraphrase.

_items.title: Check side by side before finishing
_items.body: Compare the finished paraphrase against the original once more, specifically looking for anything that still matches too closely.

title: Practical guidance: checking a paraphrase
body: Run through this list for every paraphrase in a piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: You have compared the paraphrase against the original, sentence by sentence.
No sentence structure closely tracks the original, even where words have changed.
Any phrase too distinctive to rewrite is quoted directly instead.
The source is cited, and the wording is genuinely your own.

title: Check 1: comparing a paraphrase
displayTitle: A paraphrase keeps the original's sentence structure, swapping only a few words, and cites the source. Is this an acceptable paraphrase?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Is a paraphrase that keeps the original's structure but cites the source acceptable?

_items.text: No, because the sentence structure still belongs to the original author, regardless of the citation.
_items.feedback: Yes. A citation credits the idea; it does not excuse a structure that is still effectively the original author's.

_items.text: Yes, because the source is cited correctly.
_items.feedback: Citing the source is necessary but not sufficient; the wording and structure must also genuinely be the writer's own.

_items.text: Yes, because some words have been changed.
_items.feedback: Changing a few words while keeping the same structure does not make the sentence a genuine paraphrase.

_items.text: No, because citations are not needed for paraphrases.
_items.feedback: A paraphrase does need a citation; the problem here is the surviving structure, not the presence of a citation.

_feedback.correct: Yes. The structure still belongs to the original author; a citation alone does not make it an acceptable paraphrase.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a citation does and does not excuse.
_incorrect.final: The structure still belongs to the original author; citing the source does not excuse that, and synonym-swapping does not create a genuine paraphrase.

title: Check 2: identifying surviving wording
displayTitle: A paraphrase uses a distinctive phrase from the original word for word, without quotation marks, but cites the source. What is this an example of?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does using a distinctive unquoted phrase from the original show?

_items.text: Distinctive wording surviving unattributed, because the exact phrase is used without quotation marks.
_items.feedback: Yes. A distinctive phrase used word for word needs quotation marks, however the source is cited.

_items.text: A correctly formatted citation.
_items.feedback: The citation format is not the issue; the exact phrase needs quotation marks.

_items.text: A summary rather than a paraphrase.
_items.feedback: This is still presented as a paraphrase; the problem is the exact phrase surviving unquoted.

_items.text: An acceptable paraphrase, since the source is credited.
_items.feedback: Crediting the source does not excuse an exact phrase appearing without quotation marks.

_feedback.correct: Yes. An exact phrase without quotation marks is distinctive wording surviving unattributed, whatever the citation says.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what quotation marks are for, separately from the citation.
_incorrect.final: The exact phrase needs quotation marks; the citation format, calling it a summary, and crediting the source do not resolve this.

title: Check 3: revising a paraphrase
displayTitle: In a piece of work for {{context}}, your paraphrase still follows the original's sentence order after a first attempt. What should you do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should be done when a paraphrase still follows the original's sentence order?

_items.text: Set the original aside and rewrite the idea in a different structure from memory.
_items.feedback: Yes. Rewriting from memory, in a different structure, is how surviving wording gets removed.

_items.text: Add a second citation to the same sentence.
_items.feedback: A second citation does not change the sentence structure that is the actual problem.

_items.text: Shorten the sentence so less of it matches.
_items.feedback: Shortening the sentence does not address the structure still tracking the original.

_items.text: Leave it, since the idea is correctly credited.
_items.feedback: Credit alone does not resolve a structure that still tracks the original too closely.

_feedback.correct: Yes. Rewriting from memory in a different structure is the fix for wording that still tracks the original.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what actually changes the sentence structure, rather than the citation or the length.
_incorrect.final: Rewriting from memory, in a different structure, is the fix. A second citation, shortening, or leaving it do not address the structure itself.

title: Does this reference list include opposing views?
instruction: Match each reference list description to a judgement about its range.

_items.text: A list that cites five studies all reaching the same conclusion, on a question where the field is known to disagree
A list that cites the leading study and a direct rebuttal of it, alongside supporting work
A list that cites only sources published by the same research group as the writer

_feedback.correct: Right. A reference list that cites only agreement, or only one group's own work, has not represented the field's disagreement, whatever its formatting looks like.

_incorrect.notFinal: Look again at who is being cited, not just how many sources there are. Agreement in number is not the same as a represented range of views.

title: Judging a reference list's range
instruction: Put these steps for judging a reference list's range in order.

_items.text: Note what the writer claims the research covers
List the sources actually cited and what each one covers
Check whether disagreement in the field is represented
Identify what the claimed scope implies that is missing

_feedback.correct: Right. Scope first, then what is actually there, then whether disagreement features, then what the gap between the two implies.

_incorrect.notFinal: Start from what the writer claims to cover before checking what is actually cited; otherwise you are judging the list against nothing.

title: Reading a reference list for its range
body:
{{learner-a}} is asked to check a reference list attached to an essay claiming to cover "current debate on remote work productivity". {{learner-a}} counts the sources: eleven, all recent, all from business journals. {{learner-a}} decides the list is strong because there are enough sources and they all look current.

{{learner-b}} is asked to check the same list. {{learner-b}} starts from the claim, not the count: debate implies disagreement. Reading the eleven sources, {{learner-b}} finds they all report the same finding, that remote work increases productivity, and none test or challenge it. {{learner-b}} concludes the list is one-sided: it supports a claim of debate while containing none, whatever its size and recency.

title: Four signs a reference list's range falls short
instruction: Select each card to reveal a sign a reference list's range does not match its claimed scope.

_items.title: Only agreement
_items.body: Every source reaches the same conclusion, on a question the field is known to contest.

_items.title: Only one source type
_items.body: A claim about practice is supported only by theory, or a claim about theory only by anecdote.

_items.title: Only one group's own work
_items.body: The citations all trace back to the same research team or institution.

_items.title: Scope narrower than the claim
_items.body: The writer claims a broad review but the citations cover only a narrow slice of it.

title: Four ways to identify an evidence gap
instruction: Select each heading to reveal a way to identify an evidence gap in a reference list.

_items.title: Compare the claim to the citations
_items.body: State what the writer says the research covers, then list what the citations actually cover; the difference is the gap.

_items.title: Check for a missing source type
_items.body: A claim resting only on theory with no empirical support, or the reverse, has a gap in evidence type.

_items.title: Check the date range
_items.body: A claim about a fast-moving field supported only by older sources may have a currency gap.

_items.title: Check for the obvious rebuttal
_items.body: If a well-known challenge to the claim exists and is not cited, that absence is itself a gap.

title: Checking a reference list's range
body:
Use this checklist when judging a reference list:

  1. State what the writer claims the research covers.
  2. List what the cited sources actually cover.
  3. Check whether views that disagree with the writer's own are represented.
  4. Identify anything the claimed scope implies that is missing from the list.

title: Check your understanding
body: A reference list cites eleven recent sources, all reaching the same conclusion on a question the field is known to contest. What does this most strongly suggest?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: The list is strong, because eleven sources is a large number
The list's range does not match a contested question, because it represents no disagreement
The list is strong, because all sources are recent
The list cannot be judged without knowing the authors' institutions

_feedback.correct: Right. On a contested question, uniform agreement across every cited source is itself evidence that the list's range is too narrow, not a sign of strength.
_feedback._incorrect: Count and recency do not establish range. A list that cites only one side of a known disagreement has not matched the field's actual shape, however many sources it contains.

title: Check your understanding
body: An essay claims to give "a full review of theories of motivation" but every source cited is a single textbook chapter summarising one theory. What is missing?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Nothing; a textbook chapter is a reliable source for any claim
The range does not match the claimed scope: one summary cannot support a claim of a full review
The essay needs a longer reference list, regardless of what it contains
The source is too old to be used for this claim

_feedback.correct: Right. A claim of a full review commits the writer to a range of theories and sources; one textbook summary cannot deliver on that claim, however reliable it is on its own terms.
_feedback._incorrect: The problem here is range against the claim made, not the reliability or age of the one source cited.

title: Check your understanding
body: You are judging a reference list for {{context}}. The list cites recent studies supporting the main argument, but no study that tests or challenges it. What gap does this show?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: An evidence gap: no opposing or testing view is represented
No gap, provided every cited source is itself reliable
A formatting gap, because the citations may not follow a consistent style
A currency gap, because the sources are described as recent

_feedback.correct: Right. Recency and individual reliability do not supply disagreement. A list that cites only supporting evidence leaves an evidence gap at the point where a challenge should appear.
_feedback._incorrect: Reliability and recency are not the issue here. Look at what kind of evidence is missing: anything that tests or opposes the main argument.
